sub_branches.concept: Fallacy of Unweighted Averages in Unequal Groups
details: Taking a simple unweighted average of group means ignores group size differences.
Larger groups exert a greater pull on the true overall population mean.
Weighted arithmetic mean accounts for subgroup counts or weights w_i.
evidence_or_examples: Combining Section A (30 students, avg 80%) and Section B (10 students, avg 60%) yields true weighted mean 75%, not 70%.

sub_branches.concept: Weighted Mean Formula and Physical/Financial Applications
details: Used in weighted test grading, gold alloy purity, solution concentration, and mixture blending.
Preserves total quantity and mass conservation across combined subsets.
evidence_or_examples: Academic grade calculation with assignments (30%), midterm (20%), and final exam (50%).
Mixing brass alloy Batch A (200 kg at 70%), Batch B (120 kg at 50%), and Batch C (240 kg at 45%) to get 55% concentration.

details: Combining speeds v_i over equal distances d_i requires weighted harmonic mean, not arithmetic mean.
Formula for average speed: v_avg = sum(d_i) / sum(d_i / v_i) = Total Distance / Total Time.
Simpson's Paradox occurs when aggregated group weights cause overall statistical trends to reverse.
evidence_or_examples: Traveling 100 km at 40 km/h and returning 100 km at 60 km/h yields average speed 48 km/h, not 50 km/h.

sub_branches.concept: Cluster-Column, Stacked Bar & 100% Stacked Bar Charts
details: Cluster-column charts place category bars side-by-side per group.
Stacked bar charts stack category components vertically to preserve absolute group totals.
100% stacked bar charts scale all group bars to 100% height to isolate relative percentage distributions.
evidence_or_examples: Comparing household spending (housing, food, education, healthcare) across families with different total incomes.
